title: Dynamic L7 API Gateway & Reverse Proxy
infrastructure: Cloud compute (2 gateway VMs) · Managed Redis Config Store · Managed Secret Manager · 3 application services · 3 databases
description: Design a high-performance L7 API gateway and reverse proxy. A Rate Limiter drops excess traffic before it reaches the gateways. A Load Balancer spreads requests across multiple gateway instances running on cloud compute. Each gateway verifies the client's JWT using signing/public keys fetched from a Secret Manager, then routes the request to the User, Product or Order service by URL path. Routing rules live in a shared Config Store (Redis) that the gateways watch, so rules reload live without restarting. Each service owns its own database.

tasks.title: Put a Load Balancer in front of the gateway instances
tasks.detail: Traffic must be distributed across more than one gateway. A single gateway in the path is not horizontally scalable.

tasks.title: Run at least two gateway instances
tasks.detail: Each gateway is an independent L7 reverse proxy VM. Two or more instances are required for failover.

tasks.title: Connect the Config Store to every gateway (not to services)
tasks.detail: Each gateway watches the shared Config Store so routing rules reload live without a restart. Services must not be wired directly to it.

tasks.title: Connect the Secret Manager to every gateway only
tasks.detail: Gateways fetch JWT signing/public keys from the Secret Manager. No other component needs secret access.

tasks.title: Carry 50 requests/sec of shared traffic
tasks.detail: The client should offer about 50 req/s and the gateways should split it evenly (round robin).

tasks.title: Fail Gateway VM 1 without causing failures
tasks.detail: Tearing down one gateway must not drop traffic. The Load Balancer health check should reroute to the surviving gateway and error rate should stay at zero.

tasks.title: Apply a routing change without restarting
tasks.detail: Publish a new routing configuration and confirm both gateways activate it after the propagation delay, with no restart and no failed requests.

quiz.q: Why is the Rate Limiter placed before the gateways instead of after them?
quiz.a: It rejects excess traffic with HTTP 429 as early as possible, protecting every downstream component (gateways, services and databases) from overload.

quiz.q: Why does each gateway talk to the Secret Manager directly rather than through the Config Store?
quiz.a: Secrets (JWT signing keys, TLS certificates) have a different lifecycle and access model than configuration. Gateways fetch keys at startup and on rotation; routing rules change far more often and are watched through the Config Store.

quiz.q: What happens to routing if the Config Store goes down?
quiz.a: Gateways keep their last valid routing table, surface a warning and retry. In-flight routing keeps working; only new rule versions are delayed.

quiz.q: What makes the gateway layer horizontally scalable?
quiz.a: Gateways are stateless request routers whose configuration lives in the shared Config Store and whose keys live in the Secret Manager, so additional instances can be added behind the Load Balancer without coordination.
